screens.title: Scope Definition & Authorization
screens.narratorSegment: Defining scope and securing authorization is the guardrail for every cloud penetration test. Start by listing which cloud accounts, subscriptions, regions, and specific services or resource identifiers are in scope. A vague scope risks crossing provider boundaries or impacting tenants you should not touch. Obtain explicit written permission from the client and confirm whether the cloud provider requires notification for certain tests. For example, many providers require prior approval for denial-of-service testing or scanning that resembles abuse. In practice, your Statement of Work should name account IDs, regions, allowed test windows, and an explicit list of prohibited actions such as deletion of data or stopping instances. A concrete checklist helps: include the target account numbers, permitted CLI tools and credentials, read-only versus allowed modifications, escalation contacts, and any monitoring points defenders will watch. A common misconception is that a client agreement alone is always enough; in cloud environments you may also need to inform the provider to avoid automated mitigations or account suspension. Finally, document rollback and incident contacts. The goal is to create a controlled, auditable environment where discovery and testing can proceed without accidental harm. After you finish defining scope, ask: does this SOW prevent unintended cross-account impacts?

keyIdea.title: Scope principle
keyIdea.text: A precise SOW plus provider notification prevents accidental cross-account or provider-level consequences.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Scope Definition
Process

Scope definition checklist

  1. Identify accounts and regions: include exact account IDs, subscriptions, and permitted regions.
  2. List services and resources: name specific S3 buckets, storage containers, or instances if applicable.
  3. Permission model: specify read-only or allowed modifications and test windows.
  4. Provider notifications: declare any required cloud provider approvals.
Example SOW snippet
"Authorized to enumerate IAM, list storage buckets, and perform non-destructive checks in account 123456789012 for region us-east-1. No destructive actions; no DoS testing without prior written consent from cloud provider."
Key Takeaway

Document targets precisely and verify provider rules before testing. Ambiguity risks suspension or unintended impact.

Authorization flow
Client SOW
Defines account IDs, allowed actions, and emergency contacts.
Provider Notification
Some tests require prior approval; notify to prevent automated blocks.
Incident & Rollback Plan
Agree how to respond to accidental outages and how to restore services immediately.
Common misconception
"Client authorization is always sufficient." Not always — providers can block activity or require notification, so treat provider rules as a second authorization layer.

screens.title: External Reconnaissance & OSINT
screens.narratorSegment: External reconnaissance in cloud testing targets public assets and service endpoints that reveal an organization’s cloud footprint. Start with OSINT sources—DNS records, public certificates, and search engines that index cloud-hosted web apps. Tools like Shodan can show exposed IPs or services, and DNS lookups can reveal subdomains that map to cloud-hosted applications. A concrete example: list public S3 buckets and web-facing domains. Run a DNS enumeration against the target domain, then check each discovered hostname for cloud provider headers or storage endpoints. A common mistake is relying only on simple port scans. Many cloud services sit behind load balancers or APIs that do not respond like traditional hosts. Instead, probe for cloud-specific indicators: S3-style endpoints, Azure blob naming patterns, or metadata links indicating cloud instances. When you find a public asset, record its identifier and any accessible data. Remember: do not attempt to authenticate or brute-force; external recon is about mapping what is visible without credentials. End with this question: what public resources exist that could reveal internal references or credentials if misconfigured? External Reconnaissance & OSINT means external recon maps what is publicly visible; cloud services often expose different signatures than traditional hosts.. In practical terms, find public-facing cloud assets using open sources and service-specific queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › External Recon
Definition

External reconnaissance & OSINT

Identify public endpoints, domains, and storage that reveal the cloud footprint without credentials.

Practical commands and checks
# DNS enumeration (example)
nslookup target.example.com

# Search for public S3 buckets pattern
curl -I https://my-target-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com

# Use Shodan-like queries to find exposed services
# Use web headers and certificate transparency logs to find cloud assets
Concrete example
A discovered subdomain returned an S3 endpoint header. That pointed to a public bucket containing a config file listing database endpoints. Record and report this evidence rather than downloading or changing files.
Common mistake
Treating cloud endpoints like normal hosts may miss storage patterns or API-only exposure. Look for provider-specific naming and headers.
Checklist
  • Collect domains and certificates
  • Probe for provider-specific endpoints
  • Index public buckets and storage endpoints
  • Log evidence for reporting
Key Takeaway

External recon finds the public surface. Document identifiers and avoid any authenticated probing without explicit permission.

screens.title: Internal Enumeration with Cloud CLIs & Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Internal enumeration begins once you have credentials or explicit in-scope access. Use the provider’s CLI to list resources. For AWS, the aws cli can list S3 buckets and IAM users with simple commands. Tools like ScoutSuite and Prowler automate checks across services and highlight common misconfigurations, such as public buckets or overly-permissive IAM policies. A concrete example: with read-only lab credentials, run aws iam list-users to see user identities, then aws iam list-attached-user-policies to inspect attached policies. If a policy includes wide actions or star resources, flag it for deeper analysis. Be mindful of rate limits and credential scope. A common misconception is that CLI enumeration is harmless at scale; repeated A P I calls can trigger alarms or rate-limiting and may be interpreted as abuse. Use pagination, respectful timing, and read-only permissions in a lab environment. Record outputs as proof—policy documents, bucket ACLs, and configuration dumps. Use automated auditors to prioritize findings, but always confirm results manually before reporting. Closing question: which CLI outputs would you include as proof in a report to demonstrate an overly-permissive IAM policy? In practical terms, using aws cli, az cli, scoutsuite and prowler to map resources and find misconfigurations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Internal Enumeration
Hands-on

CLI enumeration and automated auditors

Use provider CLIs to enumerate accounts and combine outputs with auditors like ScoutSuite or Prowler for prioritized findings.

Example commands (read-only lab)
aws s3 ls
aws iam list-users
aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name my-test-user
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket my-target-bucket
# Run ScoutSuite for a broad audit (lab environment)
Concrete scenario
With read-only credentials you list users and find one user has an attached policy granting iam:CreateUser and iam:AttachUserPolicy on all resources. That single discovery indicates a potential escalation path and should be documented with the policy output.
Best practices
  • Use read-only lab credentials where possible
  • Control request rate to avoid throttling
  • Validate automated findings manually
Misconception
Assuming automated auditors provide definitive proof. They are excellent for discovery but must be corroborated with raw CLI outputs for reporting.
Key Takeaway

Capture CLI policy and ACL outputs as evidence, respect rate limits, and confirm automated results before including them in reports.

screens.title: Vulnerability Identification & Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud vulnerability analysis centers on a handful of high-impact categories: IAM misconfigurations, misconfigured storage, network security rules, vulnerable applications, and insecure serverless functions. Start by classifying findings into these buckets so you can prioritize. For example, an IAM policy that allows broad actions or trusts from another role can enable privilege escalation. A concrete example is a policy granting s3:PutObject on all buckets and iam:AttachUserPolicy — that combination permits an attacker to write credentials and then attach them to another user. Misconfigured storage is often straightforward to confirm: list the bucket ACL and the public access block settings to show it is readable. Network issues like wide-open security groups or NSGs can expose management ports. A common misconception is that network-level rules alone imply immediate compromise; combine network evidence with authentication and application context. Serverless functions deserve special attention: overly permissive execution roles or insecure dependencies can give code-level access to resources. For each identified vulnerability, capture the proving commands or policy documents and propose precise fixes such as tightening resource ARNs, enabling public access blocks, or restricting trust relationships. End with: which of these categories poses the highest immediate risk in your target environment?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Vulnerability Analysis
Comparison

High-impact vulnerability categories

IAM Privilege Escalation
Look for wildcard actions or trust policies that allow role chaining and escalate privileges.
Misconfigured Storage
Public buckets or permissive ACLs can leak secrets and data that enable further compromise.
Network Misconfigurations
Security groups or NSGs with broad inbound rules expose management interfaces or services.
Concrete example
A user policy allowed s3:GetObject and iam:ListUsers. By listing users and scanning public buckets, an attacker could find credentials stored in a bucket and then use them to escalate privileges. Proof includes the policy document and the bucket ACL output.
Fix recommendations
  • Apply least privilege to IAM policies; avoid '*' in actions or resources.
  • Enable public access block and tighten bucket ACLs.
  • Restrict security groups to known IP ranges and remove open management ports.
Key Takeaway

Group findings by category and provide both evidence and precise remediation steps to defenders.

screens.title: Exploitation, Safety, and Initial Post-Exploitation
screens.narratorSegment: Exploitation in cloud assessments should be conservative and evidence-focused. Validate a finding by producing non-destructive proof: list objects in a public bucket, capture ACLs and policy documents, or show that an A P I call returns sensitive metadata. Avoid modifying or deleting resources unless explicitly permitted. For example, if you find a public S3 bucket, a safe proof is the output of aws s3api get-bucket-acl and a sampled list of object keys; do not download or delete objects without permission. When testing IAM escalation, demonstrate the path by showing the policies and trust relationships that would enable an escalation rather than attempting to create new principals. Initial post-exploitation aims to map blast radius and lateral movement potential. With a foothold, ask: can this principal access other accounts, buckets, or management APIs? Use read-only A P I calls to enumerate accessible resources and stop if you reach out-of-scope targets. A common misconception is that accessing a resource proves exploitability across the environment; always map permissions carefully. Conclude by preparing reproducible steps and commands that defenders can run to validate and remediate the issue. Your closing question: what read-only evidence will convince a defender to act immediately?

keyIdea.text: Prove vulnerabilities with read-only evidence, map lateral potential conservatively, and avoid any destructive actions unless explicitly authorized.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Exploitation & Post-Exploitation
Principle

Non-destructive validation and mapping

Demonstrate impact using read-only outputs and enumerate lateral movement potential without changing resources.

Safe proof examples
# Show bucket ACL and public access block
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket example-bucket
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket example-bucket

# Show an IAM policy attached to a role
aws iam get-role --role-name example-role
aws iam get-role-policy --role-name example-role --policy-name my-inline-policy
Post-exploitation questions
  • Can this identity access other accounts or critical buckets?
  • Do execution roles or functions expose sensitive APIs?
  • Is there sufficient logging to detect these actions?
Concrete scenario
You verify a role trust policy that allows an external role to assume privileges. Instead of assuming it, capture the trust document and the role policy as proof. Document the exact API call a defender can use to reproduce the check.
Common mistake
Attempting to perform changes to prove escalation. Always prefer evidence that can be replayed by defenders without granting yourself extra privileges.
Key Takeaway

Validate impact with read-only proofs, map lateral access cautiously, and provide reproducible remediation steps.

screens.title: Lateral Movement and Cross-Account Pivoting
screens.narratorSegment: After gaining an initial foothold in a cloud environment, an attacker focuses on lateral movement and pivoting to amplify impact. Lateral movement means using discovered credentials, role-assumptions, or misconfigurations to reach other services, accounts, or regions. For example, an attacker who finds an EC2 instance profile with a role that can assume another role in a different account may call the cloud provider's security token service to request temporary credentials. That path often relies on misconfigured trust policies or overly permissive role assumptions. Concrete example: imagine a compute instance running a service that inadvertently exposes an IAM instance profile with permission to assume a backup role in a separate account. The attacker enumerates instance metadata, extracts temporary keys, then calls the assume-role A P I to gain broader access. This is a classic cross-account pivot. A common misconception is that network segmentation alone prevents lateral movement. In cloud environments, identity and role trust relationships can bypass network boundaries. An organization might restrict network flows but still allow role assumption between accounts. That makes reviewing IAM trust policies and role chaining essential. When testing, capture evidence of each step: the A P I calls used, the temporary credentials obtained, and the scope of resources accessible. Always prefer read-only or non-destructive verification. Ask yourself: could an attacker perform the same role assumption chain with fewer steps? The core insight is that identities and trust relationships are often the easiest path to expand access, so analyze them as thoroughly as you would network paths.

When testing, capture evidence of each step: the A P I calls used, the temporary credentials obtained, and the scope of resources accessible. Always prefer read-only or non-destructive verification. Ask yourself: could an attacker perform the same role assumption chain with fewer steps? The core insight is that identities and trust relationships are often the easiest path to expand access, so analyze them as thoroughly as you would network paths.

keyIdea.title: Pivot via identity, not just network
keyIdea.text: Lateral movement in clouds frequently uses IAM trust and temporary credentials to reach other accounts or services.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Lateral Movement
Claim
Identity paths are the most common pivot routes

Excessive assume-role permissions or exposed temporary credentials let attackers jump accounts even when networks are segmented.

Step-by-step
  1. Enumerate roles, policies, and trust relationships with provider CLI or SDKs.
  2. Check instance metadata endpoints for temporary credentials when you control a VM.
  3. Test role assumption APIs for cross-account access using non-destructive calls.
  4. Record which resources become visible or accessible after assumption.
Example Scenario
An attacker reads instance metadata to obtain temporary keys, then uses the security token service to assume a backup role in a linked account. That role allows listing storage buckets, revealing sensitive data.
Annotated Flow
Cross-account role chain
Compromised VM
Attacker reads metadata and extracts temporary keys.
Assume-Role Call
STS call to assume a role with a trust policy that allows the VM's role.
New Account Access
List and read storage, databases, or management APIs.
Key Takeaway

Identity relationships can bypass network isolation. Validate trust policies, remove wildcards in assume-role rules, and monitor role assumption events in audit logs.

screens.title: Cloud-Native Security Tools and Logging
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud providers offer native logging and detection services that are central to effective assessments. Audit logs—such as AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, or Google Cloud Audit Logs—record A P I calls and management events. When configured correctly, these logs show who called which A P I, from which IP, and with which principal. Detection services like GuardDuty or Azure Security Center analyze telemetry for suspicious behavior, such as unusual role assumptions, reconnaissance patterns, or data exfiltration attempts. Concrete example: CloudTrail enabled in all regions captures an A P I call to assume a role. If GuardDuty or a similar detector flags the pattern as anomalous, defenders can investigate the source IP, time window, and subsequent actions. If CloudTrail is disabled or logs are stored with no centralized retention, an attacker may act without leaving a clear trace. That makes log configuration, retention, and cross-account aggregation critical controls. A common misconception is that simply turning on a detection product is sufficient. In practice, detection value comes from correct configuration, alert tuning, and log retention and integrity. For assessments, test whether logging is enabled, whether logs are aggregated across accounts, and whether alerts trigger on suspicious role chaining or large data transfers. In your reports, include evidence of logging gaps and clear remediation: enable multi-region logging, use immutable storage or restricted access for logs, and route findings to a centralized SIEM or security command center. The bottom-line insight is that defensive telemetry is as important as identifying vulnerabilities; without it, investigations and remediation become much harder.

keyIdea.title: Telemetry enables detection and forensics
keyIdea.text: Cloud-native logging and managed detection services provide the evidence and alerts needed to detect, investigate, and remediate attacks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Cloud Logging
Definition
Audit logs and managed detection

Audit logs record management API actions. Managed detectors analyze those logs and telemetry to surface suspicious behavior like role assumption chains or mass data reads.

Checklist
  • Is multi-region audit logging enabled and retained?
  • Are logs aggregated to a central account or SIEM?
  • Is role-assume and console-login activity monitored and alerted?
  • Are logs protected from tampering and restricted in access?
Example
GuardDuty flagged unusual data access after a role assumption. Investigation used CloudTrail events to map the API calls and time stamps, enabling quick revocation of the compromised role.
Annotated Log Example
CloudTrail-like event
{
  "eventTime": "2023-01-01T12:34:56Z",
  "eventName": "AssumeRole",
  "userIdentity": { "arn": "arn:aws:iam::111:role/CompromisedRole" },
  "sourceIPAddress": "203.0.113.12",
  "requestParameters": { "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::222:role/TargetRole" }
}
Key Takeaway

Logging and detection are only useful when enabled, centralized, and monitored. Verify configuration, retention, and alerting during assessments.

screens.title: Assessing Serverless Functions Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless functions present a different attack surface than VMs. They run short-lived code with execution roles and rely on managed services. Common weaknesses include overly permissive execution roles, insecure dependencies, and injection or insecure deserialization in function handlers. When testing serverless, prioritize non-destructive checks: inspect execution roles and invocation patterns, review environment variable contents for secrets, and perform safe input testing for injection flaws. Concrete example: a function with an execution role that allows writing to all storage buckets and invoking other functions creates a dangerous chain. An attacker who finds a way to invoke the function with malicious input might cause it to write sensitive data to an attacker-controlled bucket, or to call administrative APIs. The right test path is to enumerate the function's role and simulate invocations in a controlled lab environment rather than triggering production functions with real data. A misconception is that serverless functions are isolated by default. In reality, permissions assigned to the function govern what it can access. Also, insecure dependencies can introduce vulnerabilities because functions often include many third-party libraries. During an assessment, inspect deployment packages, environment variables, and role policies. If you must invoke functions, do so in a scoped test environment or with explicit permission that allows read-only or simulated invocations. Close with this question: if a function's role can write to storage and call management APIs, what minimal permission change would reduce risk? The answer typically points back to least privilege and removing write or invoke permissions that are not strictly required.

keyIdea.text: Serverless risk is driven by execution role permissions and insecure dependencies — tighten roles and review packages.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Serverless
Focus Areas
  • Execution role permissions and trust boundaries.
  • Environment variables and secrets management.
  • Third-party dependencies and package vulnerabilities.
  • Safe function invocation and input validation testing.
Common Mistake
Invoking production functions with test payloads without consent. That can modify data or trigger side effects. Always use a lab or explicit scope permission for invocation tests.
Key Takeaway
Review roles and packages. Testing should emphasize inspection and non-destructive checks, with controlled invocations when authorized.
Example: Inspect function role and env
# List function configuration (lab account)
aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name my-function

# Check the execution role
aws iam get-role --role-name MyFunctionRole

# Inspect environment variables
aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name my-function --query 'Environment.Variables'
Use these read-only calls in a lab environment to reveal role ARNs and environment variable names. Do not invoke functions that process production data unless explicitly authorized.

screens.title: Effective Reporting and Remediation Guidance
screens.narratorSegment: An assessment is only valuable if its findings lead to corrective action. Effective reporting organizes discoveries by impact and provides proof-of-concept evidence plus clear remediation steps. Start each finding with a concise description: what you did, the vulnerable resource, and the concrete impact. Include evidence such as A P I call logs, CLI output, or sanitized configuration snippets. For example, show the bucket ACL output that proves public read access and include the exact command you used to retrieve it. Prioritize findings by both likelihood and impact. An open storage bucket containing sensitive files is typically high-priority because it allows immediate data exposure. An overly permissive assume-role policy is high impact even if the exploit path requires multiple steps, because once chained it can lead to account takeover. Provide clear remediation: remove wildcard permissions, enable multi-region logging, restrict role trust policies, and rotate any exposed credentials. A misconception is that long technical appendices alone convince operators. In practice, an executive summary with risk levels, an itemized remediation plan, and prioritized action items speeds response. Also include reproducible non-destructive steps for validation so the client can confirm fixes without reintroducing risk. Close with a reflective question: which single configuration change would stop the highest-impact exploit you found? Your report should make that change obvious and achievable.

keyIdea.title: Actionable findings win fixes
keyIdea.text: Provide clear evidence, prioritized risk, and precise remediation steps so defenders can quickly and safely remediate vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Reporting
Report Structure
  1. Executive summary with prioritized risks.
  2. For each finding: description, impact, evidence, remediation.
  3. Reproduction steps (non-destructive) and verification checks.
Evidence Types
  • CLI output or API event records (sanitized).
  • Policy snippets showing wildcards or excessive actions.
  • Logs showing role assumptions or data reads.
Example Remediation Item
Replace Allow Action: '*' on resource '*' with specific actions and resource ARNs. Remove unnecessary assume-role trust entries and add conditions where possible.
Sample Evidence (sanitized)
# Show bucket ACL used as evidence
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket example-bucket

# Policy snippet showing wildcard actions (sanitized)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "*",
  "Resource": "*"
}
Common Pitfall
Overly technical reports without prioritized remediation. Always present a short, prioritized action list for operators and a technical appendix for engineers.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Enumerating IAM Policies (Read-Only)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough shows a safe, read-only approach to enumerate IAM policies and identify overly permissive permissions in a lab environment. Begin by configuring the CLI with lab credentials that have read-only rights. The goal is to list users, inspect attached policies, and retrieve policy documents for analysis—never to modify resources. Concrete walk-through: first run the command to list users. Then list policies attached to a selected user and retrieve the policy document for each managed or inline policy. Pay attention to statements that allow all actions or all resources: these are red flags. For example, look for an action entry that shows a wildcard or a resource set to an asterisk. That could let an attacker perform broad operations if they obtain higher-level credentials. A common misconception is that seeing a read-only credential prevents escalation. Read-only credentials can still reveal resource names, ARNs, and configuration files in storage that contain secrets. An attacker can use read-only results to locate credentials or misconfigurations that enable privilege escalation. When you document findings, include the exact read-only commands used and sanitized snippets of policy JSON showing the problematic statements. Close with a verification step: after recommended remediation, re-run the same read-only commands to ensure the wildcard actions or broad resource access are removed. This completes a safe, evidence-based lab assessment.

keyIdea.title: Inspect policies, don't assume safety
keyIdea.text: Read-only enumeration reveals risky permissions and clues to escalation paths; document commands and sanitized evidence for remediation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › IAM Lab
Objective
Enumerate IAM policies using read-only commands

Use a lab account with read-only credentials. Capture policy documents and flag wildcards in actions or resources.

Commands (read-only)
# Configure CLI with lab read-only credentials
aws configure

# List IAM users
aws iam list-users

# List managed policies attached to a user
aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name my-test-user

# Get an inline policy for a user
aws iam get-user-policy --user-name my-test-user --policy-name my-inline-policy

# Retrieve a managed policy document (sanitized)
aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:policy/my-policy-name --version-id v1
Common Pitfall
Do not run destructive commands in the lab that change policies. Your goal is enumeration and analysis only unless the SOW explicitly allows modifications.
Analyzing a policy document
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
This sanitized policy shows a wildcard action and resource. Flag it as critical and recommend replacing wildcards with least-privilege actions and resources.
Verification
After remediation, rerun the same read-only commands to confirm that wildcard actions and permissive resources were removed and that role trust policies are tightened.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's reinforce the three core concepts that tie this chapter together. First, cloud penetration testing focuses on identity and configuration rather than only network exploits. Misconfigured IAM policies or trust relationships are often the simplest path to escalate privileges and pivot across accounts. Second, cloud-native telemetry and managed detection services are central to defense and forensic analysis. If audit logs and detection are missing or misconfigured, an attacker can act with much less chance of detection. Third, ethical and legal safeguards are non-negotiable: obtain explicit authorization, define a clear scope, and avoid destructive testing. These safeguards protect both the assessor and the client, and they prevent unintentional cascading impacts across tenants. Keep these three ideas in mind as you work through labs and reports: identity-first thinking, telemetry validation, and rigorous authorization and safety practices.

keyIdea.title: Three anchors for practice
keyIdea.text: Identity focus, telemetry, and ethics are the guiding principles for cloud assessments.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Key Concepts
Identity-First Assessment

Prioritize IAM, trust policies, and role permissions—these often unlock broader access in cloud environments.

Telemetry & Detection

Ensure logs are enabled, aggregated, and monitored. Detection systems only help when configured and retained correctly.

Ethics & Scope

Obtain written authorization and provider notification as required. Use least-privilege test credentials and avoid destructive actions unless explicitly permitted.

Summary

Cloud assessments combine identity analysis, telemetry validation, and documented, authorized testing to find and fix high-impact misconfigurations safely.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep four practical reminders front of mind during cloud testing. First, always define and verify scope with explicit account and service boundaries. Second, use provider CLIs and auditing tools in read-only mode to enumerate resources and policies unless the SOW grants wider permissions. Third, prioritize fixes that remove wildcards in IAM policies and tighten role trust. Finally, include detection and logging checks in every assessment; if logs are missing or misconfigured, recommend immediate changes to enable detection and forensic capability. These reminders help you run safe, focused assessments that produce the evidence defenders need to remediate risk quickly. What to Remember means scope, read-only enumeration, least-privilege remediation, and telemetry checks make assessments useful and safe.. In practical terms, short reminders to guide your next assessment. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Remember
Confirm Scope

A clear SOW and provider notifications prevent accidental provider-impacting activity and legal exposure.

Enumerate Read-Only

Use CLI and auditing tools in read-only mode to gather evidence without changing state.

Least Privilege

Replace '*' actions and resources with specific, minimal permissions and add conditions where possible.

Final Thought

A safe, prioritized, and evidence-backed approach reduces risk and increases the likelihood that findings are remediated quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Cloud environments change how we test for security. In this lesson you will learn a practical, methodical approach to cloud penetration testing that emphasizes scope, authorization, and non-destructive verification. We will treat cloud platforms as A P I-driven ecosystems where misconfiguration and identity problems are often the highest risk. You will see how reconnaissance shifts from classic network scanning to cloud-aware enumeration with provider CLIs and automated auditors. I will show concrete commands used to list buckets and IAM users, and explain how tools like ScoutSuite and Prowler speed discovery while still requiring care. Why this matters: cloud misconfigurations often expose sensitive data or permit privilege escalation without traditional network exploits. A single overly-permissive policy, or a public storage bucket, can be faster to abuse than finding a remote code bug. You will also learn safety rules: always get explicit written authorization, observe provider rules, and prefer read-only, non-destructive tests to avoid service disruption. As we proceed, keep a mental checklist: define scope, enumerate carefully, prioritize identity and storage findings, exploit safely, and report clearly. Think about a recent cloud outage you read about: how could careful scope and non-destructive testing have prevented unintended impact?

Over these two screens you will see concrete, verifiable objectives that align with cloud testing practices. First, you will learn to define the scope and authorization requirements for a cloud test. This means articulating which cloud accounts, regions, services, and resources are allowed, and ensuring written permission from the client and any required provider notifications. Second, you will become fluent with cloud provider CLIs and automated auditors to enumerate resources. Knowing how to use the aws cli or az cli to list storage, compute, and IAM objects is a practical skill that speeds discovery. Each objective card also maps to measurable actions. You will practice finding common misconfigurations, like public storage buckets or permissive security groups, and you will practice identifying IAM privilege escalation paths. Finally, you will learn to prepare reports that include proof-of-concept, impact statements, and prioritized remediation. These report skills are essential because good testing ends with actionable fixes, not just a list of problems. Keep these outcomes in mind as the yardstick for successful practice and assessment.

This second objectives screen completes the practical skillset you will practice. First, you will learn to perform safe, basic exploitation of common cloud vulnerabilities. That means demonstrating read-only proofs like accessing open storage or showing how a permissive policy could allow an escalation path, rather than making destructive changes. Second, you will become familiar with cloud-native defensive tools and logging—how CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, or Google Cloud Audit Logs can show an attacker’s trail and how missing logs weaken detection. Next, you will study ethical and legal boundaries: what must be included in a Statement of Work and when cloud providers require notification. You will also practice respecting rate limits and least-privilege for testing credentials. Finally, you will gain the ability to identify and communicate non-destructive remediation steps for IAM and storage risks. Together these objectives combine technical enumeration skills with pragmatic safety and reporting practices that reflect real-world cloud assessments.

Defining scope and securing authorization is the guardrail for every cloud penetration test. Start by listing which cloud accounts, subscriptions, regions, and specific services or resource identifiers are in scope. A vague scope risks crossing provider boundaries or impacting tenants you should not touch. Obtain explicit written permission from the client and confirm whether the cloud provider requires notification for certain tests. For example, many providers require prior approval for denial-of-service testing or scanning that resembles abuse. In practice, your Statement of Work should name account IDs, regions, allowed test windows, and an explicit list of prohibited actions such as deletion of data or stopping instances. A concrete checklist helps: include the target account numbers, permitted CLI tools and credentials, read-only versus allowed modifications, escalation contacts, and any monitoring points defenders will watch. A common misconception is that a client agreement alone is always enough; in cloud environments you may also need to inform the provider to avoid automated mitigations or account suspension. Finally, document rollback and incident contacts. The goal is to create a controlled, auditable environment where discovery and testing can proceed without accidental harm. After you finish defining scope, ask: does this SOW prevent unintended cross-account impacts?

External reconnaissance in cloud testing targets public assets and service endpoints that reveal an organization’s cloud footprint. Start with OSINT sources—DNS records, public certificates, and search engines that index cloud-hosted web apps. Tools like Shodan can show exposed IPs or services, and DNS lookups can reveal subdomains that map to cloud-hosted applications. A concrete example: list public S3 buckets and web-facing domains. Run a DNS enumeration against the target domain, then check each discovered hostname for cloud provider headers or storage endpoints. A common mistake is relying only on simple port scans. Many cloud services sit behind load balancers or APIs that do not respond like traditional hosts. Instead, probe for cloud-specific indicators: S3-style endpoints, Azure blob naming patterns, or metadata links indicating cloud instances. When you find a public asset, record its identifier and any accessible data. Remember: do not attempt to authenticate or brute-force; external recon is about mapping what is visible without credentials. End with this question: what public resources exist that could reveal internal references or credentials if misconfigured? External Reconnaissance & OSINT means external recon maps what is publicly visible; cloud services often expose different signatures than traditional hosts.. In practical terms, find public-facing cloud assets using open sources and service-specific queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Internal enumeration begins once you have credentials or explicit in-scope access. Use the provider’s CLI to list resources. For AWS, the aws cli can list S3 buckets and IAM users with simple commands. Tools like ScoutSuite and Prowler automate checks across services and highlight common misconfigurations, such as public buckets or overly-permissive IAM policies. A concrete example: with read-only lab credentials, run aws iam list-users to see user identities, then aws iam list-attached-user-policies to inspect attached policies. If a policy includes wide actions or star resources, flag it for deeper analysis. Be mindful of rate limits and credential scope. A common misconception is that CLI enumeration is harmless at scale; repeated A P I calls can trigger alarms or rate-limiting and may be interpreted as abuse. Use pagination, respectful timing, and read-only permissions in a lab environment. Record outputs as proof—policy documents, bucket ACLs, and configuration dumps. Use automated auditors to prioritize findings, but always confirm results manually before reporting. Closing question: which CLI outputs would you include as proof in a report to demonstrate an overly-permissive IAM policy? Internal Enumeration with Cloud CLIs & Tools means combine cli commands and automated auditors; protect against rate limits and confirm automated findings manually.. In practical terms, using aws cli, az cli, scoutsuite and prowler to map resources and find misconfigurations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cloud vulnerability analysis centers on a handful of high-impact categories: IAM misconfigurations, misconfigured storage, network security rules, vulnerable applications, and insecure serverless functions. Start by classifying findings into these buckets so you can prioritize. For example, an IAM policy that allows broad actions or trusts from another role can enable privilege escalation. A concrete example is a policy granting s3:PutObject on all buckets and iam:AttachUserPolicy — that combination permits an attacker to write credentials and then attach them to another user. Misconfigured storage is often straightforward to confirm: list the bucket ACL and the public access block settings to show it is readable. Network issues like wide-open security groups or NSGs can expose management ports. A common misconception is that network-level rules alone imply immediate compromise; combine network evidence with authentication and application context. Serverless functions deserve special attention: overly permissive execution roles or insecure dependencies can give code-level access to resources. For each identified vulnerability, capture the proving commands or policy documents and propose precise fixes such as tightening resource ARNs, enabling public access blocks, or restricting trust relationships. End with: which of these categories poses the highest immediate risk in your target environment?

Exploitation in cloud assessments should be conservative and evidence-focused. Validate a finding by producing non-destructive proof: list objects in a public bucket, capture ACLs and policy documents, or show that an A P I call returns sensitive metadata. Avoid modifying or deleting resources unless explicitly permitted. For example, if you find a public S3 bucket, a safe proof is the output of aws s3api get-bucket-acl and a sampled list of object keys; do not download or delete objects without permission. When testing IAM escalation, demonstrate the path by showing the policies and trust relationships that would enable an escalation rather than attempting to create new principals. Initial post-exploitation aims to map blast radius and lateral movement potential. With a foothold, ask: can this principal access other accounts, buckets, or management APIs? Use read-only A P I calls to enumerate accessible resources and stop if you reach out-of-scope targets. A common misconception is that accessing a resource proves exploitability across the environment; always map permissions carefully. Conclude by preparing reproducible steps and commands that defenders can run to validate and remediate the issue. Your closing question: what read-only evidence will convince a defender to act immediately?

After gaining an initial foothold in a cloud environment, an attacker focuses on lateral movement and pivoting to amplify impact. Lateral movement means using discovered credentials, role-assumptions, or misconfigurations to reach other services, accounts, or regions. For example, an attacker who finds an EC2 instance profile with a role that can assume another role in a different account may call the cloud provider's security token service to request temporary credentials. That path often relies on misconfigured trust policies or overly permissive role assumptions. Concrete example: imagine a compute instance running a service that inadvertently exposes an IAM instance profile with permission to assume a backup role in a separate account. The attacker enumerates instance metadata, extracts temporary keys, then calls the assume-role A P I to gain broader access. This is a classic cross-account pivot. A common misconception is that network segmentation alone prevents lateral movement. In cloud environments, identity and role trust relationships can bypass network boundaries. An organization might restrict network flows but still allow role assumption between accounts. That makes reviewing IAM trust policies and role chaining essential. When testing, capture evidence of each step: the A P I calls used, the temporary credentials obtained, and the scope of resources accessible. Always prefer read-only or non-destructive verification. Ask yourself: could an attacker perform the same role assumption chain with fewer steps? The core insight is that identities and trust relationships are often the easiest path to expand access, so analyze them as thoroughly as you would network paths.

Cloud providers offer native logging and detection services that are central to effective assessments. Audit logs—such as AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, or Google Cloud Audit Logs—record A P I calls and management events. When configured correctly, these logs show who called which A P I, from which IP, and with which principal. Detection services like GuardDuty or Azure Security Center analyze telemetry for suspicious behavior, such as unusual role assumptions, reconnaissance patterns, or data exfiltration attempts. Concrete example: CloudTrail enabled in all regions captures an A P I call to assume a role. If GuardDuty or a similar detector flags the pattern as anomalous, defenders can investigate the source IP, time window, and subsequent actions. If CloudTrail is disabled or logs are stored with no centralized retention, an attacker may act without leaving a clear trace. That makes log configuration, retention, and cross-account aggregation critical controls. A common misconception is that simply turning on a detection product is sufficient. In practice, detection value comes from correct configuration, alert tuning, and log retention and integrity. For assessments, test whether logging is enabled, whether logs are aggregated across accounts, and whether alerts trigger on suspicious role chaining or large data transfers. In your reports, include evidence of logging gaps and clear remediation: enable multi-region logging, use immutable storage or restricted access for logs, and route findings to a centralized SIEM or security command center. The bottom-line insight is that defensive telemetry is as important as identifying vulnerabilities; without it, investigations and remediation become much harder.

Serverless functions present a different attack surface than VMs. They run short-lived code with execution roles and rely on managed services. Common weaknesses include overly permissive execution roles, insecure dependencies, and injection or insecure deserialization in function handlers. When testing serverless, prioritize non-destructive checks: inspect execution roles and invocation patterns, review environment variable contents for secrets, and perform safe input testing for injection flaws. Concrete example: a function with an execution role that allows writing to all storage buckets and invoking other functions creates a dangerous chain. An attacker who finds a way to invoke the function with malicious input might cause it to write sensitive data to an attacker-controlled bucket, or to call administrative APIs. The right test path is to enumerate the function's role and simulate invocations in a controlled lab environment rather than triggering production functions with real data. A misconception is that serverless functions are isolated by default. In reality, permissions assigned to the function govern what it can access. Also, insecure dependencies can introduce vulnerabilities because functions often include many third-party libraries. During an assessment, inspect deployment packages, environment variables, and role policies. If you must invoke functions, do so in a scoped test environment or with explicit permission that allows read-only or simulated invocations. Close with this question: if a function's role can write to storage and call management APIs, what minimal permission change would reduce risk? The answer typically points back to least privilege and removing write or invoke permissions that are not strictly required.

An assessment is only valuable if its findings lead to corrective action. Effective reporting organizes discoveries by impact and provides proof-of-concept evidence plus clear remediation steps. Start each finding with a concise description: what you did, the vulnerable resource, and the concrete impact. Include evidence such as A P I call logs, CLI output, or sanitized configuration snippets. For example, show the bucket ACL output that proves public read access and include the exact command you used to retrieve it. Prioritize findings by both likelihood and impact. An open storage bucket containing sensitive files is typically high-priority because it allows immediate data exposure. An overly permissive assume-role policy is high impact even if the exploit path requires multiple steps, because once chained it can lead to account takeover. Provide clear remediation: remove wildcard permissions, enable multi-region logging, restrict role trust policies, and rotate any exposed credentials. A misconception is that long technical appendices alone convince operators. In practice, an executive summary with risk levels, an itemized remediation plan, and prioritized action items speeds response. Also include reproducible non-destructive steps for validation so the client can confirm fixes without reintroducing risk. Close with a reflective question: which single configuration change would stop the highest-impact exploit you found? Your report should make that change obvious and achievable.

This hands-on walkthrough shows a safe, read-only approach to enumerate IAM policies and identify overly permissive permissions in a lab environment. Begin by configuring the CLI with lab credentials that have read-only rights. The goal is to list users, inspect attached policies, and retrieve policy documents for analysis—never to modify resources. Concrete walk-through: first run the command to list users. Then list policies attached to a selected user and retrieve the policy document for each managed or inline policy. Pay attention to statements that allow all actions or all resources: these are red flags. For example, look for an action entry that shows a wildcard or a resource set to an asterisk. That could let an attacker perform broad operations if they obtain higher-level credentials. A common misconception is that seeing a read-only credential prevents escalation. Read-only credentials can still reveal resource names, ARNs, and configuration files in storage that contain secrets. An attacker can use read-only results to locate credentials or misconfigurations that enable privilege escalation. When you document findings, include the exact read-only commands used and sanitized snippets of policy JSON showing the problematic statements. Close with a verification step: after recommended remediation, re-run the same read-only commands to ensure the wildcard actions or broad resource access are removed. This completes a safe, evidence-based lab assessment.

Let's reinforce the three core concepts that tie this chapter together. First, cloud penetration testing focuses on identity and configuration rather than only network exploits. Misconfigured IAM policies or trust relationships are often the simplest path to escalate privileges and pivot across accounts. Second, cloud-native telemetry and managed detection services are central to defense and forensic analysis. If audit logs and detection are missing or misconfigured, an attacker can act with much less chance of detection. Third, ethical and legal safeguards are non-negotiable: obtain explicit authorization, define a clear scope, and avoid destructive testing. These safeguards protect both the assessor and the client, and they prevent unintentional cascading impacts across tenants. Keep these three ideas in mind as you work through labs and reports: identity-first thinking, telemetry validation, and rigorous authorization and safety practices.

Keep four practical reminders front of mind during cloud testing. First, always define and verify scope with explicit account and service boundaries. Second, use provider CLIs and auditing tools in read-only mode to enumerate resources and policies unless the SOW grants wider permissions. Third, prioritize fixes that remove wildcards in IAM policies and tighten role trust. Finally, include detection and logging checks in every assessment; if logs are missing or misconfigured, recommend immediate changes to enable detection and forensic capability. These reminders help you run safe, focused assessments that produce the evidence defenders need to remediate risk quickly. What to Remember means scope, read-only enumeration, least-privilege remediation, and telemetry checks make assessments useful and safe.. In practical terms, short reminders to guide your next assessment. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
